newsitem.title: UK: TUC slams govt for opposing EU working rights.
newsitem.headline: TUC slams govt for opposing EU working rights.

text.p: Britain's Trades Union Congress (TUC) accused the government on Monday of opposing a European Union directive on working time out of a "narrow-minded resistance to all things European".
The European Court of Justice is due to rule on Tuesday on Britain's challenge to the directive, which covers working time, rest breaks and holidays and comes into effect on November 23.

The directive, 93/104/EC, was treated by EU member states as a health and safety issue, which meant it could be passed by a qualified majority. Britain argues that it is an employment issue, which requires unanimity. It abstained when the rules were passed.

The TUC said Britain is the only EU country where workers have no legal right to annual leave, and nearly 2.5 million British employees had no paid holidays. The directive gives all workers -- part-time and full-time -- three weeks leave. British workers are also made to work longer hours than their comrades around Europe, the union said. Some 31 percent of full-time employees work 46 hours per week or more, against nine percent in France and six percent in Germany.
The directive limits the working week to an average of 48 hours over any four-month period, although many exemptions are allowed, for example rail workers and doctors in training.
